summary: Okanogan NF site with two lookouts standing side by side, a 1923 D-6 cupola and a 1947 L-4 tower, staffed into the late 1980s and now a standby lookout.

facts.status_note: Kept as an emergency/standby lookout; not rented or regularly staffed since the late 1980s.

access.note: Reached by a steep, largely unshaded trail; no road access to the summit.

visit.trail_note: ~4,500 ft elevation gain to over 7,000 ft; faint trail with blowdown in burned sections, little reliable water.

events.note: Original log cabin lookout established on the summit around 1920.

TrailChick cites an undated 1920s Methow Valley Journal report naming Gwendolyn Creveling as lookout; Fire Lookout Museum gives 1923 as her specific year. No source gives 1921 specifically, so 1923 (the more specific, sourced year) is used here.
D-6 cupola-style lookout house constructed, replacing the log cabin; now used for storage.
30' timber L-4 tower erected alongside the cupola.
Last actively staffed year per TrailChick and NHLR.
Cub Creek 2 Fire interrupted a planned volunteer work party and both towers were wrapped for fire protection as a precaution.

evidence.supports: D-6 cupola built 1923, one of only nine surviving of over 200 in the Northwest; 1947 L-4 tower, last staffed 1988, now an emergency lookout.
evidence.quote: In 1947 a 30' timber tower with a 14' x 14' hip roof L-4 cab with catwalk was erected. Last staffed in 1988, it is now maintained as an emergency lookout.

evidence.supports: Log cabin established 1920; D-6 cupola built 1923, now used for storage, one of only nine of more than 200 built in the Northwest still surviving.
evidence.quote: The first lookout, a log cabin, was established on North Twentymile Peak on the Okanogan National Forest in 1920. A D-6 cupola lookout was constructed in 1923. Now used for storage, it is one of only nine remaining of more than 200 that were built in the Northwest.

evidence.supports: Site established ~1920 with log cabin; D-6 cupola 1923; L-4 tower 1947; last staffed 1988; still used as emergency lookout.
evidence.quote: In 1923, the D-6 cupola was built and actively used until 1947, when the existing 30' treated timber L-4 tower was constructed. North Twentymile was last actively staffed in 1988 and is still sometimes used as an emergency lookout.

evidence.supports: 1921 newspaper report naming Gwendolyn Creveling as the lookout for North 20-Mile mountain.
evidence.quote: Miss Gwendolyn Creveling of Winthrop will be the lookout on North 20-Mile mountain in the Methow.

evidence.supports: 2021 Cub Creek 2 Fire interrupted planned roof repairs; towers wrapped for fire protection.
evidence.quote: Unfortunately, two days before our planned work party, the Cub Creek 2 fire started and closed access up the Chewuch. When the fire spread north, N20's twin lookouts were wrapped for fire protection, just in case.

evidence.supports: Trail requires ~4,500 ft gain to over 7,000 ft, faint in spots with blowdown, little water.
evidence.quote: it does require nearly 4,500' gain and takes you above 7,000' so it's certainly not a walk in the park

evidence.supports: Named lookout personnel: Albin 1929, Heaton 1952, Crandall 1954/1958-1959.
evidence.quote: Known lookout personnel: 1923: Gwendolyn Crevling; 1929: Carl Albin; 1952: Paul Heaton; 1954, 1958-1959: Bob Crandall.

corrections.why: Both NHLR and TrailChick describe a 30-foot timber tower (~9.1 m); 42 m (~138 ft) is not supported by any source and may be a data-entry error.

notes_for_editor: Brief's height_m of 42.0 appears to be an error (likely confused with elevation or another unit) — a 30' timber tower is ~9.1m; flagged as a correction. Firelookout.com gives '1923: Gwendolyn Crevling'; TrailChick's newspaper excerpt for her is only dated to 'the 1920s' generally (not 1921 as an earlier draft stated) — fixed during verification to use the more specific, sourced 1923 date and to drop the unsupported '1921'/'for the coming season' wording. Also fixed: the story had said the 2021 Cub Creek 2 Fire 'forced an evacuation of the work crew,' but TrailChick's account says the fire closed access two days before the planned work party even started, so no one was there to evacuate; corrected to say the work party was called off.
